title_original: ‘Hexed’ review: Uninspiring Disney animation about a teen witch fails to generate a great deal of magic
excerpt_original: Hailee Steinfeld, Rashida Jones and Jodie Foster voice the studio’s latest animated original

blocks.text: Source: Disney
‘Hexed’
Dirs: Fawn Veerasunthorn, Jason Hand. US. 2026. 103mins

A daughter, mother and grandmother hash out their familial trauma in Disney’s Hexed , an animation about witches that lacks sufficient magic. Hailee Steinfeld voices the film’s rebellious young hero, who learns that she’s part of a lineage of powerful beings when she accidentally enters an otherworldly realm ruled by sorceresses. But while its refreshing to see a studio picture in which the central conflicts concern the relationships between generations of women, Hexed too easily leans on fairytale tropes, only rarely proving suitably emotional.
Rowdy, somewhat juvenile humour and an emphasis on wacky side characters

Flying into US theatres on November 25 before arriving in the UK two days later, this Disney release may continue a recent trend for the studio of underperforming original animated films over the Thanksgiving holiday, following 2022’s Strange World ($74 million worldwide) and 2023’s Wish ($255 million). Steinfeld is joined by Rashida Jones and Jodie Foster, but Hexed ’s familiar contours may depress family attendance. Streaming could ultimately be a more welcoming proposition.

Billie (Steinfeld) lives with her single mother Alice (Jones), who is overly protective, insisting that her daughter always wear a mysterious bracelet. Eventually, Billie learns the truth: the bracelet keeps her magic powers in check, while also preventing the world from discovering that she, like Alice, is actually a witch. Once Billie removes the bracelet, she is transported to the land of witches known as Hexe, which is run by the villainous Queen Celeste (Foster). But the teenager has one more shock in store: Celeste is Alice’s mother, and Billie’s grandmother.

Directors Fawn Veerasunthorn ( Wish ) and Jason Hand ( Moana 2 ) play with recognisable narrative elements, telling a story about a spirited teen who longs to break free of a controlling parent. (In addition, Billie will learn she might be the prototypical ’chosen one’ who has a mighty destiny ahead of her.) Add in rowdy, somewhat juvenile humour and an emphasis on wacky side characters, and Hexed closely resembles a slew of different adolescent animated films of the last decade.

Steinfeld brings the proper sarcasm and sincerity to Billie, who is elated to discover that she is a witch, especially once she figures out how to fly. but Hexed ’s script fails to make Billie comparably endearing or riveting. Instead, screenwriters Jared Bush and Dana Ledoux Miller settle for a pseudo-hip comedic approach, giving Billie flat one-liners without digging into her insecurities or dreams. A similar problem affects Alice, who is a cliched ’helicopter parent’. despite the maternal sweetness Jones lends the role.

The film’s animation is pleasing but rarely stunning. Hexed switches between different aspect ratios, presenting the real world in rectangular widescreen while showing Hexe in full screen, which adds some visual novelty, but this magical otherworld fails to wow. Production designer Lorelay Bové renders Hexe as overstuffed but unimaginative, and the creatures Billie encounters are pro forma comic relief. (Walton Goggins provides the voice of Beef Roger Crummchuk, a talking three-eyed feline who has plenty of attitude but not much personality.)

Hexed builds its plot around Hexe’s forthcoming Haven Moon ceremony and Celeste’s desire to consolidate her ’queendom’. But the film is most compelling when delving into the complicated childhood Alice had with her mother. Once Alice follows Billie into Hexe to rescue her, the audience learns more about how these three generations are connected by magic, even though that magic is not as potent in each woman. There’s a potentially moving metaphor in the fact that Celeste drains magical energy from others to bolster her fading power, suggesting how parents can irreparably harm their offspring by placing their needs over those of their children. Foster exudes regalness as Celeste that is mixed with a casual cruelty, but only infrequently are the full implications of these three women’s intra-family tensions meaningfully articulated.

Amidst the expected reconciliation between Alice and Billie, who will eventually recognise the sacrifices Alice made to keep her safe, there is also a pointed commentary about how a good, nurturing parent’s achievements can go unappreciated. Alice has been loving and supportive of her daughter, which leads to a twist near the end that might make the audience question cinema’s traditional notions of what a hero looks like. It’s a touching sentiment but as is the case with much of Hexed , this reveal is handled in predictable fashion, sapping the moment of its catharsis – much like Celeste sucking the magic from those around her.

Worldwide distribution: Disney
